chief_complaint: sudden excruciating abdominal pain radiating to back, pulsatile mass, and fainting in smoker
hpi_details: 72F heavy smoker presenting with sudden severe tearing back/abdominal pain, pulsatile epigastric mass, and hypotension (BP 80/50). POCUS shows 8cm AAA with retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
ideas: She thinks she severely threw out her back or tore a deep muscle while working earlier today.
concerns: She is terrified that she is dying right now on the stretcher just like her husband did when he suddenly collapsed.
expectations: She hopes the medical team can immediately give her powerful pain medication and find out what tore inside her body.
social_hx: Heavy smoker (long-standing tobacco use), social drinker, employed full-time

available_results.value: 8.0 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal hematoma

clinical_knowledge.topic: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate recognition as a surgical emergency, permissive hypotension resuscitation, and emergent transfer to the operating room for open or endovascular aneurysm repair, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating abdominal pain radiating to back, pulsatile mass, and fainting in smoker

Key HPI features: 72F heavy smoker presenting with sudden severe tearing back/abdominal pain, pulsatile epigastric mass, and hypotension (BP 80/50). POCUS shows 8cm AAA with retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

Objective/Exam findings: BP 80/50 (hypotensive shock), skin pale and diaphoretic. Abdominal exam reveals a tender, expansile, pulsatile epigastric mass. Bedside POCUS demonstrates an 8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal free fluid/hematoma.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Hypotension with a pulsatile abdominal mass — go straight to the operating room.
management_principles: SURGICAL EMERGENCY - activate the operating room and vascular/general surgery team immediately; do not delay for confirmatory CT once POCUS is diagnostic in an unstable patient

Implement permissive hypotension (target systolic BP 80-90 mmHg) with judicious IV fluids/blood products rather than large-volume crystalloid resuscitation, which can dislodge clot and worsen retroperitoneal bleeding
Activate massive transfusion protocol, secure large-bore IV access, and obtain type and crossmatch
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating abdominal pain radiating to back, pulsatile mass, and fainting in smoker

72F heavy smoker presenting with sudden severe tearing back/abdominal pain, pulsatile epigastric mass, and hypotension (BP 80/50). POCUS shows 8cm AAA with retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
reference_soap.objective: BP 80/50 (hypotensive shock), skin pale and diaphoretic. Abdominal exam reveals a tender, expansile, pulsatile epigastric mass. Bedside POCUS demonstrates an 8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal free fluid/hematoma.
reference_soap.assessment: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) with hemorrhagic shock - an immediate surgical emergency.
reference_soap.plan: SURGICAL EMERGENCY - immediate transfer to the operating room without delaying for further imaging. 1. Implement permissive hypotension (target systolic BP 80-90 mmHg) rather than aggressive crystalloid resuscitation. 2. Activate massive transfusion protocol, secure large-bore IV access, and obtain type and crossmatch. 3. Emergent open or endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) by vascular/general surgery.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical triad of ruptured AAA: sudden tearing abdominal/back pain, a pulsatile mass, and hypotension
Apply the principle of permissive hypotension during ruptured AAA resuscitation
Use bedside POCUS to confirm the diagnosis without delaying definitive surgical care
Coordinate emergent OR transfer and massive transfusion protocol activation

teaching.one_liner: A tear in a weakened aortic wall producing sudden tearing pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass, and hypotension from retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
red_flags: Hypotension with a pulsatile abdominal mass — go straight to the operating room

must_ask.say: Did the pain start suddenly and feel like tearing?
Does the pain go through to your back?
Do you feel lightheaded or like you might pass out?
Do you smoke, or have you smoked in the past?
Has anyone ever told you that you have an aortic aneurysm?

history.answer: My stomach and back started hurting terribly all of a sudden, and I feel so weak and dizzy.
It hit me completely out of nowhere about two hours ago while I was sitting on the couch.
It is right in the middle of my upper belly, and it has stayed right there without moving anywhere else.
Yes, the pain shoots straight through to my middle and lower back, like something is tearing inside.
It feels like a constant, terrible tearing and ripping pressure deep inside my belly.
It is a complete ten out of ten, the most unbearable agony I have ever experienced.
Nothing makes it any better, and even taking a deep breath or trying to move makes it worse.
No, I have never had any pain like this in my entire life.
I felt very sick to my stomach from the sheer agony and threw up a little bit of clear liquid once, but no blood.
I had a regular bowel movement this morning before this began, with no diarrhea, constipation, or dark blood.
No, I haven't had any fever, sweating from a cold, or chills at all.
No, my eyes and skin are not yellow, and my bowel movements and urine look normal in color.
No, it does not burn when I pee, I don't go frequently, and there is no blood in my urine.
Yes, I got lightheaded and broke out in a cold sweat, and when I stood up to call for help, I passed out on the floor.
No, I haven't had any spotting, bleeding, or unusual discharge, and I went through menopause over twenty years ago.
My chest feels fine without any tightness, though I am breathing fast because my stomach hurts so intensely.
I only had a slice of toast and a cup of black coffee for breakfast, nothing greasy, and no alcohol.
No, I haven't taken any aspirin, ibuprofen, or stomach pills recently.
No, I've never been told I have an irregular heart rhythm, atrial fibrillation, or blood clots.
Yes, right when the pain hit, I felt this strange, strong throbbing lump pulsing right in my upper belly.
No, no doctor has ever mentioned that I had an aneurysm or an enlarged blood vessel.
I thought I must have severely thrown out my back or ripped a muscle at work, because the pain tore straight through to my belly and made me pass out.
I'm terrified that I'm dying right here, just like my husband did when he suddenly collapsed at home.
I don't have any major chronic health problems, and I don't see a doctor regularly.
I have never had any surgeries or needed to stay in a hospital before.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have smoked about a pack of cigarettes every day for around fifty years.
I might have one glass of wine when dining out with friends once a month, but that is all.
I work full-time as an administrative manager at an accounting firm and live with my husband.
My father passed away from a heart attack in his sixties, but no one in my family had an aneurysm that I know of.

exam.finding: Elderly woman appearing acutely ill, pale, diaphoretic, and in severe distress due to excruciating pain.
Blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, temperature 36.4°C, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Skin is pale, cool, and diaphoretic with delayed capillary refill, but without cyanosis, jaundice, or ecchymosis.
Radial and femoral pulses are rapid and weak bilaterally without asymmetry or deficit.
Abdomen is flat without distension, visible surgical scars, or flank ecchymosis.
Hypoactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants with no audible abdominal bruits.
Tender, expansile, pulsatile mass palpated in the epigastrium and central abdomen.
No true rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal wall rigidity.
Negative Murphy sign with no focal right upper quadrant tenderness or inspiratory arrest.
No tenderness at McBurney point; psoas and obturator signs are negative.
Normal rectal sphincter tone with brown stool in the ampulla; no palpable masses or gross blood.
